## The Glory by the River Chebar: Ezekiel's Call and the God Who Finds You in Exile (Ezekiel 1–3)
*The heavens open over a labor camp, and a fugitive God comes looking.*

**Text:** Ezekiel 1–3 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 1:1; Ezekiel 2:3–4; Ezekiel 3:1–3; Psalm 137:1–4; Revelation 4:2–3; John 1:14

The worst place to lose God is the place He was supposed to live. Ezekiel is a priest, trained his whole life to stand in one building, on one hill, in one city, where the presence of God had a fixed address — and by the fifth day of the fourth month in the fifth year of King Jehoiachin's exile, roughly 593 BC, he is nine hundred miles from that building, sitting in a deportation settlement on an irrigation ditch in Babylon. He is thirty years old, the age a priest begins to serve. He will never serve, not the way he trained to. The temple is still standing, but he cannot reach it, and within seven years it will not be standing at all. He is a priest with no altar, in a country that is not his, among people who have decided God does not travel. And the heavens open.

We should feel how impossible that opening is before we admire it. The exiles did not expect it. The whole ancient world had taught them not to.

### I. The God Who Travels to the Ditch (Ezekiel 1:1–28)

Read the first verse the way a deportee would have read it. “In the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, as I was among the exiles by the Chebar canal, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God” (Ezekiel 1:1). Notice where he is. Not on Zion. By a canal — a Babylonian public-works project, dug by conquered labor to move water for an empire that had just crushed his nation. The place itself was a monument to defeat. Psalm 137 was written from this exact geography: “By the waters of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion… How shall we sing the LORD's song in a foreign land?” (Psalm 137:1, 4). That last question is not rhetorical. It is theology. The song belonged to a place, and the place was gone.

The theology of the ancient Near East was territorial. Every god had turf. Marduk owned Babylon; Chemosh owned Moab; a defeated god stayed behind with his defeated people, or he was simply defeated. To be dragged east was to be dragged out from under the reach of your God — carried past the border of His care into the territory of a stronger deity who had just proven it. The exiles believed a version of that. And some of us believe a quieter version of it still. We believe God is available at the address where things were working — the marriage before it cracked, the church before it split, the country before it turned — and that when the building burns and the map changes, we have somehow moved beyond His jurisdiction. We do not say it out loud. We live it. We stop praying because we assume we have crossed a border God does not cross.

Then the storm comes out of the north — the direction Babylon itself invaded from, the direction every threat had come from — and God rides in on it. A great cloud, fire flashing, brightness around it. Four living creatures, each with four faces and four wings; wheels beside them, wheels within wheels, their rims full of eyes; and over their heads a platform like crystal, and above the platform a throne of sapphire, and on the throne “a likeness with a human appearance” (Ezekiel 1:26). John will see the same throne and the same rainbow around it in Revelation 4:2–3. The machinery is not the point, and we should resist the urge to solve it like a puzzle. The point is that the throne has wheels. The God of the immovable temple has arrived on a mobile chariot in the last place His people thought He could go. He is not confined to Jerusalem. He was never confined to Jerusalem. He came to the ditch.

- **A. Glory is not comfort** — Ezekiel's response to the vision is not warmth but collapse: “Such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell on my face” (Ezekiel 1:28). The presence of the holy has always leveled the person it visits — Isaiah undone in the temple, John falling as though dead. It does not first console. It first undoes. A glory that only comforted would not be the glory of God.
- **B. The exile is not the end of the address** — The wheels mean the covenant did not burn with the city. The God who could be found in the temple can be found by a broken priest on a foreign canal, which means He can be found by you where you actually are, not where you were when it worked. That is either the most obvious truth in Scripture or the one we have most quietly stopped believing.

### II. Eat the Scroll Before You Speak the Word (Ezekiel 2:1–3:15)

Then God commissions him, and the commission is brutal in its honesty. “Son of man, I send you to the people of Israel, to nations of rebels, who have rebelled against me… The descendants also are impudent and stubborn” (Ezekiel 2:3–4). No promise of a good hearing. No projected growth. The opposite: “whether they hear or refuse to hear (for they are a rebellious house), they will know that a prophet has been among them” (Ezekiel 2:5). The measure of the prophet will not be results. It will be presence and faithfulness — that a true word was spoken, whether or not it was received. That phrase, “son of man” — ben-adam, son of dust — lands on Ezekiel more than ninety times in this book. In the same breath God shows him the throne of heaven, He names him a mortal made of clay. The vision does not inflate the messenger. It shrinks him to scale. A man who has genuinely seen the throne does not come away impressed with himself.

And before Ezekiel says a single word to anyone, God hands him a scroll and makes him eat it. It is written on front and back — no room left for additions of his own — “and there were written on it words of lamentation and mourning and woe” (Ezekiel 2:10). Then: “Son of man, eat whatever you find here. Eat this scroll, and go, speak to the house of Israel… Then I ate it, and it was in my mouth as sweet as honey” (Ezekiel 3:1, 3). The word of judgment tasted sweet going down and would turn bitter in the living of it — the same word John eats in Revelation 10, sweet in the mouth and bitter in the belly. The message had to become part of the man before it could come out of the man. He could not deliver grief he had not swallowed. There is no shortcut around this. The prophet who has not eaten the lament will only ever perform it. He will hold the scroll at arm's length and read it to people from a safe distance, and they will hear that it never cost him anything, and they will be right.

- **A. Faithfulness is measured before the audience answers** — God defines success as speaking, not as being received. “Whether they hear or refuse to hear.” The outcome is God's; the obedience is Ezekiel's. That order is the only thing that frees a man to tell the truth, because a man measured by reception will always shave the word down to what the room can take.
- **B. The word must be internalized before it is announced** — The eaten scroll is the whole doctrine of the messenger in one image. We have built a machinery for broadcasting messages no one has swallowed — the shared post, the borrowed line, the conviction rented for the length of a sentence. Ezekiel is fed grief before he is trusted with speech. The order is not optional.

### III. The Watchman on the Wall of a Post-Christian City

Then God sets him down among the exiles at Tel-abib, by the Chebar, and he sits there “overwhelmed among them seven days” (Ezekiel 3:15). Stunned. Silent. Before he prophesies a single word he grieves for a week. And I have skipped that week myself — I have wanted the platform and the message and the effect, and I have not wanted the seven silent days of eating the lament until it became mine. We want the vision without the collapse and the word without the swallowing. Ezekiel gets neither. He gets the throne, and the dust, and the scroll, and the week on the ground.

Here is where the exile stops being ancient. The philosopher Charles Taylor, in his 2007 book *A Secular Age*, describes what he calls the immanent frame — a way of living in the modern West in which God is no longer the assumed background of a life but one option among many, and often not the plausible one. Five hundred years ago, in the West, unbelief was nearly impossible; now belief is the harder thing, held against the grain of a whole culture that runs on the assumption He is not there. The building where God had a fixed address, culturally speaking, has been vacated. The Christian in the modern West is not living in Christendom's Jerusalem. He is a priest by a Babylonian canal, and the surrounding theology insists that God stayed behind with a civilization that no longer exists. The temptation is to spend our lives grieving the lost address and waiting to move back — to treat every year the culture drifts further as one more year in a captivity that will surely end soon. But Ezekiel does not get to move back. The temple falls. God comes to the ditch. The wheels were always the point.

And the mission God gives the exile is not comfort or nostalgia. It is the watchman's word. “Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me” (Ezekiel 3:17). The church in a post-Christian culture is not called to grieve the temple that burned until grief becomes its whole identity. It is called to stand on the wall of a city that does not want a watchman and speak anyway, whether they hear or refuse to hear. That is not a diminished calling. It is the original one.

- **A. The exile is our address, not our exception** — We keep treating cultural marginality as an emergency to be reversed, a detour off the real road. But exile is the normal water the church has swum in for most of its history, and the same God who rode the storm-chariot to Chebar is not stranded when the culture stops assuming Him. The wheels go where the sheep go.
- **B. The glory that fell here becomes the Word made flesh** — The likeness on the throne, the human appearance seated in the fire, is the God who would not stay in one building. Six centuries later that glory came all the way down: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father” (John 1:14). The verb there is pitched a tent — tabernacled. The glory Ezekiel saw on wheels came down and camped in the exile with us. It has done it before. It can do it in your ditch.

God finds you in the ditch you can't leave.

## The Watchman's Blood: The Cost of Silence in a Post-Christian Culture (Ezekiel 3:16–27; 33:1–20)
*If the wall has a watchman and he sleeps, the city dies in his silence.*

**Text:** Ezekiel 3:16–27; 33:1–20 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 33:6; Ezekiel 33:11; Ezekiel 3:18; Acts 20:26–27; 2 Corinthians 5:20; Ezekiel 18:23

There is a kind of silence that kills. Not the silence of the persecuted, whose mouth is stopped by force — that silence is a wound. This is the silence of the watchman who has a mouth and a wall and a warning and chooses sleep. God gives Ezekiel a role that is easy to sentimentalize and hard to live: the man on the wall of the city, the one who sees the army first and either sounds the horn or does not. And God attaches to that role a sentence so severe it should stop the throat of anyone who has ever been trusted to tell the truth. If the watchman sees the sword coming and says nothing, the person dies for his own sin — “but his blood I will require at the watchman's hand” (Ezekiel 33:6). Required. The word is a courtroom word. There is a ledger, and the silent watchman is on it.

### I. The Office on the Wall (Ezekiel 3:16–21; 33:1–9)

God frames the watchman as a wartime necessity, not a poetic flourish. “If I bring the sword upon a land, and the people of the land take a man from among them, and make him their watchman, and if he sees the sword coming upon the land and blows the trumpet and warns the people” (Ezekiel 33:2–3). The watchman's job is single and clear: see the danger, sound the horn. He is not asked to win the battle or persuade the crowd. He is asked to blow the trumpet. Everything hinges on that one act. And God draws two clean lines through it. If the watchman warns and the people ignore him, “their blood shall be upon their own head” and “you will have delivered your soul” (Ezekiel 33:4–5). If the watchman stays silent, the person still dies for his own iniquity — the sin was real, the sword was earned — “but his blood I will require at the watchman's hand” (Ezekiel 33:6).

Hold both truths at once, because our age can only hold one at a time. The dying man is responsible for his own sin — the culture that says no one may ever warn anyone, that treats every warning as an assault on a free adult, gets that half and stops there. And the silent watchman is responsible for his silence — the culture that blames every bad outcome on the messenger who dared to speak gets the other half and stops there. Ezekiel is given both, unresolved, held in tension. “So you, son of man, I have made a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me” (Ezekiel 33:7). The warning is not the watchman's opinion. It is from God's mouth, and the watchman is the pipe, not the source. That is what makes the silence damnable rather than merely disappointing. He is withholding something that was never his to keep — sitting on a word God spoke, editing God's mouth down to what the room prefers.

- **A. Two responsibilities, both real** — The hearer answers for his response; the watchman answers for his warning. Modernity insists these cancel each other, that if the hearer is free then the watchman is off the hook. Ezekiel insists they coexist. Both stand at the judgment. The freedom of the one does not erase the duty of the other.
- **B. The message is from God's mouth, not the watchman's** — “You shall give them warning from me.” The prophet is not editorializing or moralizing from his own store of opinions. He is relaying. Silence, then, is not humility about one's limited perspective. It is theft of a word entrusted to be spoken.

### II. The God Who Takes No Pleasure in Death (Ezekiel 33:10–20)

And then, before we can turn the watchman's office into a weapon — before we can make it about the righteous man on the wall condemning the crowd below — God exposes His own heart under it. The exiles have collapsed into fatalism: “Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away in them. How then can we live?” (Ezekiel 33:10). They have decided the sentence is fixed, the account closed, the case lost. God answers with an oath and a plea in the same breath, and it is one of the most tender sentences in the prophets. “Say to them, As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live; turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel?” (Ezekiel 33:11). The horn on the wall is not sounded by a God who wants the city to fall. It is sounded by a God who takes no pleasure in a single death and swears it on His own life. As I live — He stakes His own existence on His unwillingness that they die.

This is the engine under the whole book, and it changes how we read every hard word in it. The same God who requires the watchman's blood for his silence is the God who begs the doomed to turn. The severity and the mercy are not in tension; they are the same love running in two directions. And He insists the door is genuinely open, both ways. “The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him when he transgresses… and as for the wickedness of the wicked, he shall not fall by it when he turns from his wickedness” (Ezekiel 33:12). No past sin is too deep to turn from; no past righteousness is a bank account to coast on. The people hear this and call it unfair — “the way of the Lord is not just” (Ezekiel 33:17) — and God turns it back on them: it is your ways that are not just. The mercy that lets a lifelong sinner turn at the end and live is the same mercy that will not let a lifelong-decent man presume on a record. You cannot keep one and discard the other. They come from the same heart.

- **A. The warning is mercy, not cruelty** — “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked.” The horn is love in a hurry. A God who wanted them dead would simply let the watchman sleep — no oath, no plea, no repeated turn back, turn back. The urgency of the warning is the proof of the affection behind it.
- **B. The door swings both directions** — The wicked who turns lives; the righteous who presumes dies. This offends our instinct for ledger-keeping precisely because it refuses to let anyone bank their past — neither the sinner to despair of it nor the decent man to rest on it. Grace and warning are the same door.

### III. The Watchman the Modern Church Fired

Here is the confession the modern church needs to make, and I have to make it first, because I have preached to be liked, and I know the exact taste of trimming a true word down to a comfortable one and calling the trimming love. We have quietly retired the office. In a culture that treats any warning as an act of violence — that hears “turn from your way and live” as hatred, as an imposition on another person's self-definition — the watchman has learned to blow no horn. We have decided, without ever deciding it out loud, that the loving thing and the warning thing are opposites, that to warn is to fail to accept. Ezekiel 33 says they are the same thing. The most loving act available to the man on the wall is the horn no one wants to hear. Silence is not the higher road. Silence, when you can see the sword, is the abdication with blood on it.

The apostle Paul understood he stood in Ezekiel's office. In Miletus, saying goodbye to the Ephesian elders around AD 57, knowing he would not see their faces again, he says, “Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all, for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:26–27). That is Ezekiel's language exactly — innocent of blood, because he did not shrink, because he declared the whole thing and not merely the parts that flattered. Paul knew that a gospel edited down to what the audience already wanted was not mercy. It was the watchman's silence wearing a smile. The whole counsel — the sword as well as the door, the wrath as well as the welcome — is what love owes the person on the road. And Paul refused to shrink from it because he loved them, not despite loving them. Shrinking would have been the failure of love, not its expression.

And underneath the whole office, making it bearable, stands the reason a man can blow the horn at all without being crushed by it. The blood the watchman fears — the blood required at his hand — has already been answered by blood freely shed. The watchman does not stand on the wall as the executioner, or even as the judge. “Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20). Implore. Beg. The watchman does not stand on the wall to condemn the city. He stands there because the King has already paid to save it, and the horn he blows is not first the announcement of the sword but the announcement that the gate is open, that the God who takes no pleasure in death has done everything a God can do to make life possible. To stay silent about that — to let a friend walk toward the sword because warning him would be awkward — is not gentleness. It is the cruelest thing a watchman can do. It is loving your own comfort more than his life.

- **A. Silence disguised as tolerance is abandonment** — We renamed cowardice as respect and cruelty as acceptance. The person who never warns his friend has not honored his freedom; he has stopped loving him enough to interrupt his dying. The unwarned man is not more free. He is only more alone.
- **B. The warning only makes sense because the Shepherd bled** — The horn announces a rescue already accomplished. The watchman is not the judge on the wall; he is the ambassador of a King who took the blood himself, who was Himself required at no one's hand but gave His life freely so the warned might live. That is why we implore rather than condemn.

Warn them, or their blood answers.

## The Siege Acted Out: When the Prophet's Body Becomes the Sermon (Ezekiel 4–5)
*A numb people will not hear a word, so God makes them watch one.*

**Text:** Ezekiel 4–5 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 4:1–3; Ezekiel 5:5; Ezekiel 5:8; Ezekiel 4:12–15; Jeremiah 19:10–11; Hebrews 10:31

There is a stage of denial that words can no longer reach. The exiles in Babylon in the years before 586 BC had built a comfortable lie, and comfortable lies are the hardest kind to dislodge because they carry the weight of hope. Jerusalem would stand, the temple was untouchable, God would never let His own city fall — it had God's name on it, David's throne in it, the ark's memory behind it. Ezekiel had spoken against that lie. Jeremiah, back in the city itself, was speaking against it. It bounced off. The people had gone deaf to the word. So God stops asking Ezekiel to say it and commands him to become it. For over a year the prophet's own body — lying bound on his side, cooking over dung, shaving his head with a sword — becomes the sermon a numb people might finally see. This is what happens when a culture goes deaf to the ear. God moves from telling to showing, and the showing is terrible.

### I. The Brick, the Iron Pan, and the Bound Body (Ezekiel 4)

God's first instruction is almost childlike, which is precisely the point. “And you, son of man, take a brick and lay it before you, and engrave on it a city, even Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 4:1). A clay tablet, a scratched map, a child's diorama of a siege — build siege works against it, throw up a mound, set camps, place battering rams all around. The prophet is playing with blocks in the dirt, and the passersby are meant to stop and stare. Then: “And you, take an iron griddle, and place it as an iron wall between you and the city, and set your face toward it, and let it be in a state of siege, and press the siege against it” (Ezekiel 4:3). The iron pan is the barrier between God and His city; God's face is set against it, hard as iron. The priest who once mediated God's nearness — whose whole office was to stand in the gap and bring the people close — now plays God's blockade. The mediator has become the wall.

Then Ezekiel lies down, bound, on his left side for the days God assigns and on his right for forty more, each day standing for a year of the nation's guilt — “I assign to you a number of days, 390 days… a day for each year I assign to you” (Ezekiel 4:5–6). The prophet's paralysis is the nation's paralysis. He is tied so he cannot roll over, cannot escape the position. Neither can they. Then the food, and this is where the sign turns the stomach. He is to bake his bread over human dung — “you shall eat it as a barley cake, baking it in their sight on human dung” (Ezekiel 4:12) — because in the coming siege and the exile after it the people will eat defiled bread among the nations, cut off from every clean thing. Ezekiel, a priest, whose entire formation was organized around clean and unclean, recoils. “Then I said, Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, I have never defiled myself. From my youth up till now I have never eaten what died of itself or was torn by beasts, nor has tainted meat come into my mouth” (Ezekiel 4:14). And God relents on the dung — He allows cow dung instead of human — but not on the meaning. The measured food, the rationed water, “bread by weight and with anxiety… water by measure and in dismay” (Ezekiel 4:16): this is famine staged in miniature. The starvation is coming, and the prophet will live a rehearsal of it so the people can never say they were not shown.

- **A. The iron pan is the barrier of a set face** — The priest becomes the wall between God and the city. The nearness that was the temple's whole promise — God dwelling in the midst — is now a griddle of iron with God's face hard against it. The absence is being staged in advance, so that when it comes it will not be a surprise but a fulfillment.
- **B. God bends on the method, never on the message** — He grants Ezekiel cow dung over human dung, honoring the priest's tender conscience even inside a sign of judgment. But the famine, the guilt counted day by day, the siege pressing in — none of that softens by a single ration. Mercy in the manner does not cancel the truth of the matter. God will accommodate a man's conscience and still bring the sword.

### II. The Sword, the Shaved Head, and the City at the Center (Ezekiel 5)

Then the most violent image of all. God tells Ezekiel to take a sword as a barber's razor and shave his head and his beard, then weigh the hair on scales and divide it into three parts. A third he burns in the fire in the middle of the city; a third he strikes with the sword all around it; a third he scatters to the wind — and God draws a sword out after them, chasing (Ezekiel 5:1–2). A few strands are bound into the hem of his robe, saved, a remnant — and then even some of those are pulled out and thrown into the fire (Ezekiel 5:3–4). This is not decoration. The hair is the population of Jerusalem. A third will die by plague and famine inside the walls, a third will fall by the sword around them, a third will be scattered into exile with the sword still at their backs. And the remnant is tiny, bound in a fold of cloth, and even the remnant is not automatically safe. God is doing demography with a razor.

And then God states the charge, and the charge turns on privilege, which is the part we least expect. “This is Jerusalem. I have set her in the center of the nations, with countries all around her” (Ezekiel 5:5). She was placed at the center of the map on purpose — set among the watching nations to display the character of God to the world, to be the city on a hill through which the peoples would see what it is to live under the true King. And she has done worse than the pagans around her. “And she has rebelled against my rules by doing wickedness more than the nations, and against my statutes more than the countries all around her, for they have rejected my rules and have not walked in my statutes” (Ezekiel 5:6). Therefore — and hold this — the judgment lands harder, not softer, on the privileged. “Therefore thus says the Lord GOD… I will do with you what I have never yet done, and the like of which I will never do again” (Ezekiel 5:9). Because more was given, more is required, and the failure of the city that had the light is a graver thing than the darkness of the cities that never had it. This is Jeremiah's shattered flask in the Valley of Hinnom, acted out on a prophet's own scalp: “So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel, so that it can never be mended” (Jeremiah 19:11).

- **A. The center carries the heaviest account** — Jerusalem was set among the nations to show God, and instead she outsinned them. Nearness to the light is not safety; it is a larger bill. The most exposed to grace are the most accountable for despising it. This should frighten the church long before it comforts her.
- **B. The judgment is exact, not extravagant** — Thirds measured by weight on a scale, days counted one per year, bread rationed by the shekel. God is not raging blindly, lashing out in fury. He is measuring, weighing, assigning. That precision is more frightening than rage, because it means every stroke is deliberate and every stroke is deserved. There is no excess to appeal to.

### III. The Sermon We Refuse to Watch

Here is the uncomfortable turn, and it turns first on the church, and on me. We have become experts at hearing judgment abstractly. We can discuss the wrath of God as a doctrine — a chapter in a systematic theology, an attribute to be balanced against the others, a topic for a study — and feel absolutely nothing, because abstraction is the anesthetic. Ezekiel 4 and 5 are God deliberately stripping the anesthetic away. He will not let the people keep the coming ruin at the safe altitude of a concept. He makes it a body on the ground for over a year, hair on a razor, bread weighed out in fear. The whole reason for the acted sign is that a numb people cannot be reached by a proposition, so the judgment is dragged down out of the abstract and made a thing you have to watch a man endure. The judgment is no longer abstract. That is the entire achievement of the sign, and it is an achievement of mercy toward the unfeeling.

And our generation may be the most anesthetized in the history of the world. We are endlessly informed and endlessly unmoved, scrolling past every real horror because we have seen the concept of it ten thousand times and the reality of it never — the war as a headline, the death as a number, the suffering as content between advertisements. We have the wrath of God filed under theology and the pain of the world filed under news, and neither file has a body in it. The post-Christian West assumes, on top of all this, that it has simply aged out of the category of judgment — that the God of Ezekiel belongs to a primitive stage of religion we have outgrown, a superstition of frightened ancients. But Charles Taylor, in *A Secular Age* (2007), makes an argument that should stop us: the modern moral order did not invent itself from nothing. Its convictions about human dignity, equality, and the worth of the weak are a Christian inheritance running on borrowed fuel — cut from their root and living, for now, on the stored sap in the wood. A culture that keeps the mercy while denying the God is doing precisely what Jerusalem did: living at the center, on the inheritance, while rejecting the One whose inheritance it is. And Ezekiel says the account for that does not simply evaporate because the debtor stopped believing in the creditor. It comes due. “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31).

But do not miss where the acted judgment finally points, because if you stop at the razor you have stopped short of the gospel. The prophet whose own body became the sign of coming wrath is the shadow of a greater Prophet whose body would become the sign in earnest. Jesus did not scratch a siege on a brick and lie down beside it. He entered the siege. He took the third burned in the fire and the third struck by the sword; He bore in His own flesh the wrath that the acted sign only rehearsed, so that the scattered third — the exiles chased across the earth by the sword — might be gathered instead of hunted, bound safely into the hem of the robe instead of thrown after into the flame. The iron pan set between God and the city, the hard face of judgment, was set against His own body on a Roman cross — and then, on the third day, it was taken away. Ezekiel's flesh preached the judgment from a safe distance of prophecy. Christ's flesh absorbed it, at the distance of zero.

- **A. Abstraction is the modern anesthetic** — We have made wrath a topic and suffering a feed, and felt nothing at either, because a concept has no body and a scroll of numbers has no face. God turns the coming judgment into a bound man in the dirt precisely because a numb people cannot be reached by an idea. The sign is severe, and the severity is mercy to the unfeeling.
- **B. The greater Sign entered the siege Himself** — Where Ezekiel dramatized the judgment at the distance of prophecy, Christ endured it at the distance of nothing, taking the fire and the sword into His own body so that the scattered could be gathered by the Shepherd instead of chased by the sword. The brick became a cross, and the prophet's rehearsal became the Savior's reality.

The judgment is no longer abstract.

## The Glory Departs: The Worst Judgment Is God Leaving (Ezekiel 8–11)
*Behind the doors of the temple, another god was already being worshiped — so the true God walked out.*

**Text:** Ezekiel 8–11 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 8:6; Ezekiel 8:12; Ezekiel 10:18–19; Ezekiel 11:23; Romans 1:24; Revelation 3:20

There is a judgment worse than fire, worse than the sword, worse than exile — and it is the one no one fears, because it does not look like judgment at all. It is God agreeing to leave. In the sixth year of the exile, roughly 592 BC, Ezekiel is lifted by the Spirit in a vision and set down inside the temple in Jerusalem — the one building on earth where the presence of God had a fixed address, where the glory had settled in Solomon's day and filled the house so that the priests could not stand to minister — and God gives him a guided tour of what is actually happening behind the doors while the deportees in Babylon still pin their hope to the place. Room by room, the vision peels back the facade, and what it finds is not an empty, waiting temple. It is a full one — full of the wrong gods. And then the unthinkable: the glory that had filled that house lifts up, moves to the door, hovers over the city, and goes. The worst thing that can happen to a people is not that God strikes them. It is that He honors their long-standing preference and withdraws.

### I. The Idolatry Behind the Doors (Ezekiel 8)

The tour is structured as a descent, each stop worse than the last, and the refrain repeats like a drumbeat: “you will see still greater abominations” (Ezekiel 8:6, 8:13, 8:15). First, at the north gate of the inner court, an “image of jealousy” — an idol provoking God to jealousy in His own courtyard, at His own front door. Then God says, “Son of man, dig in the wall.” Ezekiel breaks through and finds a hidden chamber, its walls covered from floor to ceiling with the carved images of crawling things and unclean beasts and idols, and seventy elders of Israel standing in the dark, each with his censer, a cloud of incense going up. The seventy — the leadership, the respectable men, the council. And God reveals the inner sentence they are speaking to themselves, the lie beneath the whole scene: “Son of man, have you seen what the elders of the house of Israel are doing in the dark, each in his room of pictures? For they say, The LORD does not see us, the LORD has forsaken the land” (Ezekiel 8:12). Read that carefully. They had already decided God was gone. They worshiped other gods in the dark because they had concluded the true God had stopped looking. Their idolatry was not the cause of their functional atheism. It was the fruit of it.

Then the descent continues. Women sitting at the north gate “weeping for Tammuz” (Ezekiel 8:14) — a Babylonian fertility deity, the god of the dying and rising vegetation year — pagan liturgy imported wholesale into the courts of the LORD. And then the deepest circle, the innermost court, between the porch and the altar, in the most sacred working space of the entire temple: twenty-five men “with their backs to the temple of the LORD, and their faces toward the east, worshiping the sun toward the east” (Ezekiel 8:16). Backs to the sanctuary. Faces to the creature. That is the anatomy of every idolatry laid bare in a single posture: not the absence of worship, but its redirection — the body still bowing, the incense still burning, the object swapped for the sun. The temple was busy. The incense was thick. The elders were present, devout, engaged. And every act of it was aimed at something that was not God, inside a building that still had His name over the door and His altar in the middle.

- **A. The lie is “God does not see”** — “The LORD does not see us.” Every hidden idolatry rests on a functional atheism, a practical bet that God has stopped looking and the room is empty of Him. We sin in the dark room of pictures because we have quietly concluded the light went out — and then we build our new gods to fill a house we decided He had already left.
- **B. Idolatry is redirected worship, not absent worship** — Backs to the sanctuary, faces to the sun. The men were not irreligious; they were intensely religious, just aimed at the creature. A full temple can be a far emptier place than an abandoned one, because the abandoned building at least tells the truth about who is not there.

### II. The Glory Lifts and Leaves (Ezekiel 9–11)

So the glory begins to move, and Ezekiel records it in slow, agonizing stages, because God does not storm out. He leaves reluctantly, by degrees, as though giving the city every possible moment to notice He is going and call Him back. First the glory of the God of Israel “had gone up from the cherub on which it rested to the threshold of the house” (Ezekiel 9:3). Up off its resting place above the ark, out to the doorway. Then a man clothed in linen is sent through the city to put a mark on the foreheads of all who “sigh and groan over all the abominations that are committed in it” (Ezekiel 9:4) — a mark of preservation set on the grieving in the very middle of the judgment; those who mourned the idolatry are spared the sword. Then the glory moves again: “Then the glory of the LORD went out from the threshold of the house and stood over the cherubim. And the cherubim lifted up their wings and mounted up from the earth before my eyes as they went out” (Ezekiel 10:18–19). The wheels from chapter 1 return — the mobile throne, the eyes on the rims — and it is preparing to travel. They pause at the east gate of the LORD's house. And then the final stage, the sentence that should make the whole book fall silent: “And the glory of the LORD went up from the midst of the city and stood on the mountain that is on the east side of the city” (Ezekiel 11:23).

The mountain on the east side of the city is the Mount of Olives. The glory stops on the exact ridge from which, six centuries later, another descent and another ascent would be measured. But for now it stops on the hill east of Jerusalem and looks back one last time at a temple full of the wrong gods, and then it is gone from the city entirely. And here is the mercy folded inside the horror, spoken to the very exiles who thought losing the temple meant losing God. To the deportees by the Chebar, the ones the people back in Jerusalem despised as the abandoned ones, God says: “Though I removed them far off among the nations, and though I scattered them among the countries, yet I have been a sanctuary to them for a while in the countries where they have gone” (Ezekiel 11:16). The glory that left the building did not leave the people. It went where they went. The wheels always meant the same thing. God is not trapped in a room, and He will not stay in a room that has locked Him out — but He also will not lose the humble, scattered ones who still want Him. He became their temple in the ditch.

- **A. God leaves slowly, by stages** — Cherub to threshold, threshold to the east gate, east gate to the mountain outside the city. The withdrawal is unhurried, a grief drawn out over three deliberate movements, each one a last chance for someone to notice He is leaving and cry out. A God in a hurry to abandon would not pause three times. He pauses because leaving is the last thing He wants.
- **B. The departed glory becomes a sanctuary in exile** — The same God who abandons the polluted temple becomes “a sanctuary for a while” to the scattered and marginal. The presence relocates to the humble, never to the institution that presumed on it. The building that assumed it owned God loses Him; the exiles who assumed they had lost Him get Him back.

### III. The Judgment That Feels Like Freedom

Here is the terror the modern West cannot see, and I have to name it in myself before I name it anywhere else. We assume the worst judgment must be God's intervention — the fire, the plague, the sword, the dramatic stroke from heaven. Ezekiel 8 through 11 says the worst judgment is God's departure, and departure does not feel like judgment. It feels like freedom. It feels like nothing happening, like the pressure finally lifting, like getting away with it. The elders in the dark chamber did not experience God's absence as a catastrophe. They experienced it as permission — “The LORD does not see us” was not their despair, it was their license. When they finally got the God-shaped silence they had been living toward, it did not arrive as thunder. It arrived as quiet. And that is exactly the mechanism the apostle Paul names in Romans 1: the wrath of God revealed not as lightning from the sky but as release, as being handed over. “Therefore God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity” (Romans 1:24). Three times in that one chapter the terrible refrain — God gave them up, God gave them over, God gave them up. The judgment is being left alone to have exactly what you insisted on wanting.

A post-Christian culture is not, first of all, a persecuted church waiting for rescue. It may be a culture whose long request is finally being honored — a civilization that spent generations, quietly and then openly, asking to be left alone with its own preferred gods, and is now, without noticing, getting its wish. The absence of thunder is not the absence of judgment. Sometimes the silence is the judgment. And the church is not standing safely outside this. A congregation can keep the whole apparatus — the building, the schedule, the incense of activity, the seventy respectable elders on the council — and have long since turned its back to the sanctuary and its face to the sun of the culture, and it can fail to notice the glory ever left, because leaving does not slam a door. It lifts to the threshold. It pauses. It lifts again, hoping to the last that someone grieves.

But the same Mount of Olives where the glory paused on its way out is the hill from which the risen Christ ascended, and the angels standing there made a promise about the direction of travel: “This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11). The glory that departed east returned — in a body, in a manger, in a carpenter, in the Word made flesh who “dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory.” The God who would not stay in a temple that locked Him out is the God who now stands outside the door of every heart and every church and does the opposite of walking away: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20). The glory that left Jerusalem because it was shut out is the glory that will not force the door — and will not stop knocking. That is the whole tension of grace in one image: He honors the lock, and He keeps knocking.

- **A. God's judgment can arrive as permission** — “God gave them up.” The absence of thunder is not innocence acquitted; it may be the sentence itself carried out — a people quietly handed over to the gods they preferred, given exactly what they asked for. Being left alone is the quietest wrath and the heaviest, because it feels like winning.
- **B. The departed glory returns as the knocking Christ** — The glory that paused on Olivet came back in flesh, ascended again from the same hill, and now stands outside the door knocking rather than storming out. He will not stay where He is shut out; He also will not stop asking to be let in. The Shepherd who left the temple is the Shepherd at the door.

The worst judgment is God leaving.

## The Soul That Sins: Personal Responsibility and the Open Door (Ezekiel 18:1–32)
*You are not doomed by your father, and you are not saved by your past — turn, and live.*

**Text:** Ezekiel 18:1–32 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 18:4; Ezekiel 18:20; Ezekiel 18:23; Ezekiel 18:32; Ezekiel 36:26; Romans 6:23

A people who believe they are doomed will not repent, because repentance is pointless when the sentence is fixed. The exiles in Babylon had a proverb, and the proverb was a theology, and the theology was an alibi wearing the clothes of humility. “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge” (Ezekiel 18:2). Translate it out of the metaphor: our grandfathers sinned, we inherited the verdict, the exile is a genetic sentence handed down, and there is nothing left for us to do but rot in a punishment someone else earned. It sounds like a confession of solidarity. It is actually the most comfortable position available to a guilty people, because if you are only paying for your fathers' crimes, then you are not responsible for your own, and if the outcome is already fixed and inherited, then turning is a waste of breath. Fatalism and self-exemption are the same coin. God devotes an entire chapter to demolishing the proverb, and the demolition ends not in condemnation but in the tenderest plea in the whole book.

### I. The Soul That Sins Shall Die (Ezekiel 18:1–4)

God bans the proverb outright, by oath. “As I live, declares the Lord GOD, this proverb shall no more be used by you in Israel” (Ezekiel 18:3). Then He plants the principle that will replace it: “Behold, all souls are mine; the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son is mine: the soul who sins shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4). The Hebrew word running through the chapter is nephesh — the whole living person, the breathing self, the life, not some ghost trapped inside the body. Every nephesh belongs to God directly and individually. There is no inherited account passed down the bloodline, no ancestral verdict you are born already carrying, no way to hide behind the generation before you or the generation after. Each living person stands before God as himself, uncovered.

Then God builds the case across three generations, and the structure is deliberate, almost legal in its care. A righteous man who does justice, who does not oppress, who gives his bread to the hungry — he shall surely live (Ezekiel 18:5–9). His son, violent, an idolater, a shedder of blood — he shall die; “his blood shall be upon himself” (18:10–13). And that wicked man's son, who sees all his father's sins that he has done, and considers, and does not do likewise, but does justice — he shall not die for his father's iniquity; “he shall surely live” (18:14–17). Three generations, three separate verdicts, and no transfer in either direction, up or down. God states it as a principle so it cannot be missed: “The soul who sins shall die. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father, nor the father suffer for the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself” (Ezekiel 18:20). You cannot inherit guilt. You also — and this is the edge we always drop — cannot inherit innocence. The account is yours, and only yours.

- **A. Every nephesh belongs to God directly** — “All souls are mine.” There is no bloodline to hide behind, no ancestral verdict to blame, no generational fate to shelter under. Each person stands before God as an individual self, not as a line item on a family ledger someone else wrote.
- **B. Guilt does not transfer — and neither does righteousness** — Three generations, three verdicts, no inheritance. The wicked father's righteous son lives; the righteous father's wicked son dies. This principle cuts both ways with equal force, and the second edge — that no one's decency is bankable — is the one we always let fall.

### II. The God Who Has No Pleasure in Death (Ezekiel 18:21–32)

Then the door opens, and it opens both ways, and this is where the chapter becomes almost unbearable in its mercy. “But if a wicked person turns away from all his sins that he has committed and keeps all my statutes and does what is just and right, he shall surely live; he shall not die. None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him” (Ezekiel 18:21–22). None of them. Not reduced. Not held on file. Not remembered. And then God asks the question that pries open His own chest and shows the reader His heart: “Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23). The Judge is arguing against His own courtroom on behalf of the accused. The One with every right to carry out the sentence is pleading with the condemned to make the sentence unnecessary.

But the door swings the other direction too, and God will not let us keep only the half that comforts. “But when a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice and does the same abominations that the wicked person does… none of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered” (Ezekiel 18:24). No coasting. No spiritual pension, no retirement account of past obedience to draw down. The past does not save you any more than it damns you — the record, good or bad, is not the point; the direction you are facing now is the point. And when the people cry out that this is not fair — “The way of the Lord is not just” (18:25) — God turns their complaint right back onto them: is it not your ways that are not just? It is precisely His justice that lets the murderer turn at the eleventh hour and live, and refuses to let the lifelong-decent man presume he is owed a seat. The chapter ends not with a gavel but with a plea, and it is one of the softest sentences God ever speaks in all of Scripture. “Why will you die, O house of Israel? For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live” (Ezekiel 18:31–32).

- **A. The door opens to the worst of us** — “None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him.” The wicked who turns is not put on probation with a suspended sentence; his record is erased. This is the logic of the gospel itself, spoken plainly six centuries before Calvary made it possible.
- **B. The past saves no one who presumes on it** — The righteous who turns to injustice loses the entire prior account. Grace forbids both the despair that says my past disqualifies me and the complacency that says my past secures me. You cannot bank yesterday's obedience against today's turning away.

### III. Neither Your Trauma Nor Your Ancestry Gets the Last Word

Here is where this ancient chapter walks straight into the modern room, and I have to sit down in it too, because I am the last person exempt. Ours may be the most determinist age since the exile itself. We have manufactured new versions of the sour-grape proverb, and the new versions are more persuasive than the old one because they sound like science and sound like compassion at the same time. My father did this to me, so this is what I am. My upbringing wired me this way, so I cannot be otherwise. My conditions, my chemistry, my inheritance, my formation, my history — the whole modern vocabulary of explanation quietly hardens into a modern vocabulary of exemption, and the transition happens so smoothly that no one notices the point where understanding a wound became excusing everything downstream of it. And I know this temptation from the inside, not from a distance. I was raised without a father. There is a version of that fact I could carry as a permanent alibi — a sour grape my father ate that has set my teeth on edge for a lifetime, an explanation for every failure I would rather not own. Ezekiel 18 will not let me hold it that way. The wound is real. It is not a verdict. “The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father.”

And yet — and this is where honesty has to cut deeper than the culture wants and deeper than the individualist wants — Ezekiel 18 is not a naive gospel of the self-made will, the pull-yourself-up sermon that tells a broken man he simply needs to choose harder. The chapter ends with a command to “turn,” and the same prophet knows the human heart cannot manufacture its own turning out of nothing. That is exactly why chapter 18's command becomes chapter 36's gift. The command is: “Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit” (Ezekiel 18:31). The promise, eighteen chapters later, is the answer to that impossible command: “And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). What God commands in chapter 18, God supplies in chapter 36. Personal responsibility is real, and it is total, and it is also — left to itself — insufficient, because a heart of stone cannot command itself to become flesh. The God who orders the turning is the God who works the turning.

This is the exact fault line running under the whole modern West, the one Charles Taylor traces in *A Secular Age* (2007): a culture that wants the full dignity of the responsible, self-authoring individual and the full comfort of the excused, determined victim at the same time — and cannot have both from within its own resources, because the two accounts contradict each other and neither one, alone, can bear the weight of a real human life. Ezekiel gives us both, held together without collapsing — but only because there is a cross standing at the center holding them. The soul that sins shall die; that is the wage, stated flat, and Paul says it in the same plain terms: “For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:23). The death Ezekiel names, Christ absorbed. The new heart Ezekiel promises, Christ gives by His Spirit. The open door of chapter 18 turns out to be a Roman cross and an empty tomb. You are responsible. You are also not abandoned to your responsibility. The command and the gift meet in one Person. Turn.

- **A. Explanation is not exemption** — The modern languages of trauma, wiring, chemistry, and inheritance describe the wound truly, and then quietly convert the true description into a total alibi. Ezekiel honors the wound fully and refuses the alibi entirely, and it holds both in the same breath without softening either.
- **B. The command becomes the gift in Christ** — “Make yourselves a new heart” (18:31) is answered by “I will give you a new heart” (36:26). The turning God commands is the turning God enables, through the death and the Spirit of the Shepherd who bore the wage of sin Himself so the heart of stone could be traded for a heart of flesh.

Turn, and live.

## The Shepherds Who Fed Themselves: The True Shepherd Comes for His Sheep (Ezekiel 34:1–31)
*The men hired to feed the flock ate the flock — so the Owner is coming down to feed them Himself.*

**Text:** Ezekiel 34:1–31 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 34:2–4; Ezekiel 34:11–12; Ezekiel 34:15–16; Ezekiel 34:23–24; John 10:11; Luke 15:4

The most dangerous man to a flock is not the wolf. It is the shepherd who has learned to live off the sheep. The wolf, at least, is honest about being a predator; the flock can smell him coming and scatter. The bad shepherd wears the uniform of a protector and does the work of one, and the sheep follow him right up to the moment he sells them. Ezekiel 34 is God's indictment of the leaders of Israel — the kings, the priests, the prophets, the whole ruling class that stood over the covenant people — and He delivers it under the oldest and most tender image in all of Scripture for those set over the people of God: the shepherd. David was a shepherd; the LORD is a shepherd; the psalms are full of the green pastures and the still waters and the rod that comforts. And the charge God brings is not that these men attempted a hard job and came up short. The charge is that they inverted the job entirely. They were placed over the flock to feed the flock, and they fed on it instead. And when God has finished the indictment, He does the one thing no institution on earth ever expects its critic to do: He fires the whole class and announces that He will do the job Himself.

### I. The Shepherds Who Ate the Flock (Ezekiel 34:1–10)

The indictment is precise, and every clause is a job description read backward. “Ah, shepherds of Israel who have been feeding yourselves. Should not shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat, you clothe yourselves with the wool, you slaughter the fat ones, but you do not feed the sheep” (Ezekiel 34:2–3). Eat the fat. Wear the wool. Butcher the healthy ones. Everything a shepherd receives from the flock, they took; nothing a shepherd owes the flock, they gave. Then God specifies the neglect, and every item on the list is about the vulnerable, without exception: “The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up, the strayed you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought, and with force and harshness you have ruled them” (Ezekiel 34:4). The failure is not incompetence measured in some abstract, general way. It is failure at exactly the point where power meets weakness. The strong sheep they could use — the productive, the connected, the ones who could feed the shepherd back. The weak, the sick, the strayed, the lost — the ones with nothing to give upward — they abandoned, because a self-feeding shepherd has no use for a sheep that cannot fund him. The vulnerable are always the first line item cut when leadership becomes self-supply.

And the result is a flock scattered, hunted, and eaten: “So they were scattered, because there was no shepherd, and they became food for all the wild beasts” (Ezekiel 34:5). Notice the reason the flock scattered. Not rebellion, not their own wandering hearts — here the reason is stated flatly: because there was no shepherd. They scattered because they were unshepherded, undefended, left in the open. The predators got precisely what the shepherds failed to guard. So God pronounces sentence on the leaders in words that should freeze the blood of anyone who has ever held a position over God's people: “Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will require my sheep at their hand and put a stop to their feeding the sheep. No longer shall the shepherds feed themselves. I will rescue my sheep from their mouths, that they may not be food for them” (Ezekiel 34:10). Required at their hand — the exact accounting language of the watchman's blood back in chapter 33. And the possessive is everywhere: my sheep. The flock was never theirs to consume. It was God's, entrusted to them on loan, and He is auditing the books.

- **A. The bad shepherd inverts the job, not merely fails it** — Placed there to feed, they feed on. Eating the fat, wearing the wool, slaughtering the healthy. The sin is not weakness at a hard task; it is the deliberate turning of a sacred trust into a private food supply. That is a betrayal, not a shortfall.
- **B. The test of a shepherd is the weakest sheep** — The weak, sick, injured, strayed, and lost are the whole list of the neglected, and they are the whole test. Power reveals its true aim at the point of the powerless. A shepherd who tends only the sheep who tend him back has already betrayed the office, however impressive the flock still looks from the road.

### II. “I Myself Will Search” (Ezekiel 34:11–24)

Then the verb changes, and the entire chapter pivots on a single pronoun repeated for emphasis. “For thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out” (Ezekiel 34:11). Not a better delegate. Not a reformed council. Not a committee to review shepherding practices going forward. God Himself, in the first person, twice for weight. “As a shepherd seeks out his flock when he is among his sheep that have been scattered, so will I seek out my sheep, and I will rescue them from all places where they have been scattered on a day of clouds and thick darkness” (Ezekiel 34:12). And then God takes the exact list of what the false shepherds neglected in verse 4 and reverses it, item by item, in verse 16: “I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed, and I will bind up the injured, and I will strengthen the weak.” Every single failure named in the indictment is answered by God in His own person. Where they abandoned, He gathers. Where they starved the flock, He feeds it. “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I myself will make them lie down, declares the Lord GOD” (Ezekiel 34:15). The remedy for corrupt shepherds is not better management. It is God descending into the field.

And then, with the first-person pronoun still ringing in the air, God says something that should not fit alongside it and yet does. Having just declared that He Himself, personally, will shepherd the flock, He announces one shepherd — a single man, in the line of David. “And I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David, and he shall feed them: he shall feed them and be their shepherd. And I, the LORD, will be their God, and my servant David shall be prince among them” (Ezekiel 34:23–24). David has been dead for four centuries by the time Ezekiel speaks these words. This is not the resurrection of the old king; it is the promise of the King the old David only ever pointed toward, the greater Son of David who would sit on a throne that does not end. So we are left with two claims lying side by side and apparently in tension: God Himself will be the shepherd, and God will set one Shepherd, His servant, over the flock. The claims do not compete. They wait. They wait for a single Person in whom both are true at once — one Shepherd who is somehow also God come down to seek. Six centuries later a man stands in Jerusalem and says, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). The pronoun kept its promise. I myself became one shepherd, and the one Shepherd was Himself.

- **A. The rescue is God in the first person** — “I, I myself will search.” The answer to corrupt shepherds is not a reform program but the Owner Himself coming into the field on a day of clouds and thick darkness. God refuses to fix the flock from a safe distance or through better delegates. He comes down into the mud after the lost.
- **B. God Himself and one Shepherd, both at once** — “I myself will be the shepherd” and “my servant David shall feed them” stand side by side, and the tension resolves only in Christ, who is both the God who seeks the scattered and the Shepherd who lays down His life for them. The two shepherds of Ezekiel 34 are one Person at Bethlehem.

### III. The Flock in a Culture of Self-Feeding Shepherds

Here is the sentence I have to say slowly, because I stand inside the office being indicted, not outside it commenting on it. Every pastor, every leader set over the people of God, is meant to read Ezekiel 34 as a mirror before he ever reads it as history. The temptation of the self-feeding shepherd did not die out in 586 BC when Jerusalem fell. It has only grown more sophisticated, better dressed, harder to name. A whole ministry can be constructed around the shepherd rather than the sheep — his platform, his brand, his numbers, his comfort, his legacy — with the flock quietly repositioned as the resource that funds the enterprise. And the entire operation can be conducted in the vocabulary of service the whole time, so that the man doing it can preach on servant leadership on Sunday and consume the servants by Tuesday and never feel the contradiction. The fat and the wool now arrive as influence, applause, security, reach — but it is the same meal at the same table. And the test God gives is exactly unchanged across the twenty-six centuries: what happens to the weak, the sick, the strayed, the lost — the sheep who cannot feed the shepherd back, who bring nothing upward, who only cost? A church that serves the strong and quietly loses the weak has already failed the audit, whatever the size of the room.

And this is where the collapse of Christendom in the West becomes clarifying rather than only mournful. For centuries the church in the West could operate as a self-feeding shepherd and get away with it entirely, propped up by cultural default, fed by a whole civilization that delivered the sheep to the pews whether or not any shepherd bothered to seek the lost. The culture did the seeking; the shepherd only had to receive. That prop is now gone, and it is not coming back. Lesslie Newbigin — the missionary bishop who spent nearly forty years in India and then returned to a thoroughly de-Christianized England, and wrote *The Gospel in a Pluralist Society* in 1989 out of the shock of it — saw it before most: the West is now itself a mission field, and the church can no longer coast on the inherited momentum of Christendom. Which means the self-feeding shepherd is at last exposed. When the surrounding culture stops delivering the flock automatically, only the shepherd who actually goes out and seeks the lost has any sheep left at all to feed on or feed. The end of Christendom is, among other things, God putting a stop to the shepherds who feed themselves — the very thing He promised in verse 10, worked out slowly across a continent.

But the weight of this chapter is not finally the indictment, however necessary the indictment is. The weight is the pronoun. “I myself will search.” The answer to every failed shepherd in the whole history of God's people is not a better program, a better structure, a better man — it is a Person who left the ninety-nine in the open country and “goes after the one that is lost, until he finds it” (Luke 15:4). Until he finds it. This is the Shepherd who did not slaughter the fat sheep for His own table but was Himself led as a lamb to the slaughter for the flock; who did not clothe Himself in the flock's wool but was stripped naked for the sheep; who did not require the flock at His own hand but gave His own hands to the nails so that the scattered — the third chased by the sword, the strayed left unsought, the lost written off — could be gathered instead of hunted, carried home on His shoulders instead of eaten. The false shepherds fed on the flock. The true Shepherd fed the flock His own body, and said, take, eat. And He is not a distant manager reviewing the field through others' reports. He is the Owner, in the mud, on a day of clouds and thick darkness, calling the lost sheep by its own name.

- **A. The self-feeding shepherd survives only under Christendom's prop** — A church that lives off the flock can coast comfortably as long as the culture keeps delivering the sheep for free. When that prop falls, as Newbigin watched it fall across the West, only the shepherd who actually seeks the lost keeps any flock at all. The exposure is severe, and the severity is mercy.
- **B. The true Shepherd fed the flock His own body** — Where the false shepherds ate the sheep, wore the wool, and slaughtered the healthy, Christ became the Lamb, was stripped of the wool, gave His hands to the nails, and goes out Himself across the open country after the one lost sheep until He finds it. The pronoun “I myself” walked all the way down into the mud after us.

The Owner is coming for His sheep.

## A New Heart and a New Spirit: God's Promise to Do What We Cannot (Ezekiel 36:16-38)
*Why the gospel is not a self-improvement plan but a heart transplant*

**Text:** Ezekiel 36:16-38 · **Supporting:** Jeremiah 31:33 · Deuteronomy 30:6 · Romans 8:7-8 · 2 Corinthians 5:17 · John 3:5-6 · Titus 3:5

We keep telling people to try harder. The church has built an entire industry on it — read more, pray more, commit more, decide harder, want it badly enough. And it has a stubborn habit of not working. The man who promised God on a hospital bed that he would change is the same man six months later, in the same sins, more discouraged than before. He did not lack sincerity. He lacked a new heart. And no amount of trying produces one. That is the thing Ezekiel was sent to say to a people who had already proved, in full view of the nations, that they could not keep covenant with God — and it is the thing a post-Christian culture, exhausted by its own self-help, most needs to hear and least wants to.

### I. The Diagnosis: A People Defiled By Their Own Way (Ezekiel 36:16-21)

The oracle does not open with comfort. It opens with an autopsy. Ezekiel is in Babylon, a deportee among deportees, somewhere around 586 BC with the news of Jerusalem's fall freshly landed among the exiles. The temple is rubble. The covenant looks dead. The people who had been told they were the treasured possession of God are now scattered across a foreign empire, and the obvious conclusion — the one the exiles were surely drawing in their own hearts — was that God had failed them. And God explains, through his prophet, exactly why it happened, and it is not the answer they wanted. "Son of man, when the house of Israel lived in their own land, they defiled it by their ways and their deeds. Their ways before me were like the uncleanness of a woman in her menstrual impurity" (Ezekiel 36:17). The Hebrew word is *niddah* — ceremonial defilement, the thing that cannot enter the holy place, the thing that renders a person unfit for the presence of God. Israel had not merely broken a set of rules. They had made themselves ritually and morally unfit to stand where God dwells. The problem was not their circumstances. The problem was their nature.

- **A. The exile was deserved, and God says so plainly.** "So I poured out my wrath upon them for the blood that they had shed in the land, for the idols with which they had defiled it" (Ezekiel 36:18). There is no softening here, no suggestion that Babylon overreached or that God was harsh or that the punishment outran the crime. The diagnosis is honest before the cure is offered — and we are the people who want the cure without the diagnosis. We want the new heart without first admitting the old one was stone.
- **B. The deeper scandal was God's name among the nations.** When Israel was scattered, the watching nations did not conclude that Israel had sinned. They concluded that Yahweh was weak — a local deity who could not protect his own people, defeated along with them by the gods of Babylon. "These are the people of the LORD, and yet they had to go out of his land" (Ezekiel 36:20). Read that carefully. The exile had become a public slander against the holiness of God. His people, by their sin and their scattering, had made his name look small among the nations. Hold that, because it is about to become the hinge of everything that follows.

### II. The Cure: A Sovereign Cleansing for the Sake of His Name (Ezekiel 36:22-32)

What God says next should stop us cold. "It is not for your sake, O house of Israel, that I am about to act, but for the sake of my holy name, which you have profaned among the nations" (Ezekiel 36:22). Read it twice. The most generous promise in the entire book — new heart, new spirit, cleansing, homecoming, fruitfulness — is grounded not in Israel's worth but in God's name. This is grace stripped of every flattering motive we would quietly assign it. He is not saving them because, deep down, they are lovable. He is not saving them because he saw something redeemable in them that the exile had not quite erased. He is saving them because he is holy, and his holiness will not finally be slandered among the nations by the failure of his own people. The motive of salvation is entirely outside us. That is not an insult. That is the only ground on which grace could ever be secure — because a salvation grounded in our worth could be lost the moment our worth ran out, and ours ran out at the walls of Jerusalem.

Then the promise itself, and it is staggering in its sequence. "I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean from all your uncleannesses, and from all your idols I will cleanse you. And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes and be careful to obey my rules" (Ezekiel 36:25-27). Count the verbs. I will sprinkle. I will give. I will remove. I will put. I will cause. Every active verb in the sentence belongs to God. There is not one thing on that list the people contribute, negotiate, or trigger. In the old covenant the demand had been, walk in my statutes — and they could not. In this promise God takes the very command they had failed and makes himself the one who fulfills it in them: I will cause you to walk. The human contribution to the whole transaction is to be the patient on the table. Not the surgeon. Not the assistant. The patient, unconscious, being operated on.

- **A. This is the new covenant, and Ezekiel is not alone in announcing it.** The prophet Jeremiah, his older contemporary preaching from inside Jerusalem before it fell, had already named the same reality: "I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts" (Jeremiah 31:33). Not on tablets of stone held at a distance, but on hearts, from the inside. And Moses, centuries earlier at the very edge of the promised land, had promised something the law itself could not deliver: "the LORD your God will circumcise your heart" (Deuteronomy 30:6) — the law confessing, in its own closing chapters, that it could never be kept by people whose hearts were uncircumcised. Three witnesses across the whole sweep of the Old Testament, one verdict. The problem was never the commands. The commands were good. The problem was the heart that received them.
- **B. The heart of stone is not a metaphor we can outgrow by effort.** The apostle Paul, reading this same anthropology, states the diagnosis in its hardest form: the mind set on the flesh "is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God" (Romans 8:7-8). Cannot. Not merely will not — cannot. A stone heart does not need better information or stronger motivation or a more compelling incentive. It needs replacement. A corpse cannot be coached into standing. And so the gospel, when you finally see it clearly, is not God grading our improvement and rewarding the ones who tried hardest. It is God performing a transplant we could never schedule, for a name we could never honor, to display a glory that was never ours to begin with.

### III. The Cost of Believing This in a Self-Improving Culture

Here is where this lands on us, and it costs. We live downstream of a civilization that has made the autonomous, self-creating individual its highest good. The sociologist Robert Bellah named it precisely in his 1985 study *Habits of the Heart* — expressive individualism, the conviction that the deepest truth about a person is found by looking inward, that the self is something you author rather than receive, and that the one unforgivable sin is letting anyone else tell you who you must become. That instinct did not stay in the culture. It soaked into the church, and it changed the gospel we preach without anyone voting on it. We now preach a Christianity of decision, of willpower, of the better version of yourself that is just one more commitment, one more conference, one more accountability app away. And it is, at the root, a flat denial of Ezekiel 36. It assumes the heart is basically sound and needs only better direction. Ezekiel says the heart is stone and needs a funeral before it can need anything else.

I have preached the lighter version myself. I have stood in a pulpit and handed exhausted people a longer to-do list and called it grace. I have told a man drowning in the same sin for the tenth straight year to simply choose differently, as though the choosing were the one strategy he had somehow never thought to try. That is not the gospel. That is the law with a worship band behind it. And it leaves people exactly where the exiles were — defiled by their own way, ashamed that trying did not fix it, and now carrying the extra weight of assuming the failure is a failure of effort. It is not a failure of effort. It is the predictable result of asking a stone heart to feel.

- **A. The early church fought this exact battle and settled it.** When Augustine prayed in his *Confessions*, written around 397 AD, "Command what you will, and give what you command," the British monk Pelagius was scandalized. Surely, Pelagius reasoned, God would never command what a person cannot perform; if God commands holiness, then holiness must be within our natural power to achieve. It was a reasonable, humane-sounding, and utterly deadly instinct — the same instinct alive in every self-help gospel since. The controversy that followed ran for years and was finally settled against Pelagius at the Council of Carthage in 418 AD, and reaffirmed at the Second Council of Orange in 529 AD. What was at stake was nothing less than Ezekiel 36. Can God justly command a new heart and then be the very one who supplies it? The church, reading its Bible, said yes. He gives what he commands. The whole gospel hangs on that one sentence.
- **B. The new heart is Christ's gift, sealed by his Spirit.** When Jesus told Nicodemus, a ruler and teacher who had spent his whole life trying harder than everyone around him, "unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God" (John 3:5), he was quoting Ezekiel back to Israel's own teacher — water and Spirit, cleansing and new birth, the exact pairing of 36:25-27. And he expected Nicodemus to recognize it: "Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?" Paul makes the same truth personal and final: "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come" (2 Corinthians 5:17); we are saved "not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit" (Titus 3:5). The stone heart that Ezekiel promised would be removed was carried to a cross and buried. The Spirit that Ezekiel promised would be poured in was poured out at Pentecost. The owner did not renovate the old heart. He gave a new one, at a price he paid himself.

If you have spent your life trying to want God more and failing, the failure is not the end of the story. It may be the beginning of it. Because the promise was never that you would generate a new heart by wanting it badly enough — that is precisely the thing a stone heart cannot do. The promise was that he gives what he commands, and the only people who ever actually receive it are the ones who have finally stopped pretending they could supply it themselves. So the question is not whether you have tried hard enough. The question is where your trust finally rests tonight — on the will you keep promising to fix, or on the God who buries hearts of stone and raises hearts of flesh in their place. That question should unsettle the strong long before it comforts the weak.

He gives what he commands.

## The Valley of Dry Bones: Resurrection Hope for a People Who Say Their Hope Is Lost (Ezekiel 37:1-14)
*When the word of God is preached over what everyone has already buried*

**Text:** Ezekiel 37:1-14 · **Supporting:** Genesis 2:7 · John 11:43-44 · Romans 4:17 · 1 Corinthians 15:52 · Ephesians 2:1-5 · Romans 10:17

There is a particular kind of death the church rarely names from the platform, because it is the death of hope itself. Not the funeral. The aftermath. The slow settling of a person, a marriage, a congregation, a whole civilization into the quiet conviction that whatever was once alive is not coming back. It does not weep anymore.
