It has moved past weeping into a flat, reasonable resignation. "Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost; we are indeed cut off" (Ezekiel 37:11). That is not a man in the acute stage of grief. That is a man who has finished grieving and drawn his conclusions. And it is into exactly that deadness — not the fresh wound but the old, settled certainty of death — that God brings his prophet and asks the only question that matters in a valley like this.

### I. The Valley: Death Total, Old, and Public (Ezekiel 37:1-3)

The vision begins with God taking him by force. "The hand of the LORD was upon me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of the LORD and set me down in the middle of the valley; it was full of bones" (Ezekiel 37:1). Ezekiel does not wander into this scene; he is set down in the middle of it, surrounded, unable to look away. Then a detail the prophet clearly wants us to feel: "And he led me around among them, and behold, there were very many on the surface of the valley, and behold, they were very dry" (Ezekiel 37:2). Very many. Very dry. He is made to walk through it deliberately, up one row and down the next, forced to register both the scale and the finality. These are not the freshly fallen, still recognizable, still mournable. Bones go dry when the death is old, the flesh long gone, the scavengers long finished, the hope long abandoned. To an exile around 586 BC, this was no abstraction. It was the battlefield seen the day after — Judah cut down, her armies slaughtered, her people scattered, the covenant nation reduced to scattered remains bleaching on open ground. The scene is not a poem. It is a diagnosis.

- **A. God asks the question instead of answering it.** "Son of man, can these bones live?" (Ezekiel 37:3). It is an almost cruel question to ask a man standing in a valley of dry bones — unless the one asking intends to do something about it. And that is the whole point. Every honest, sane, natural answer is no. Bones do not reassemble themselves. Dry bones do not remember how to be bodies. The dead stay dead, and everyone who has ever buried someone knows it in their body.
- **B. Ezekiel refuses both despair and false optimism.** "And I answered, O Lord GOD, you know" (Ezekiel 37:3). It is the perfect reply, and it took a prophet to find it. Not "no, they cannot" — that would fence God in with the limits of what is natural. Not "yes, of course they can" — that would cheapen the death, pretend the bones were not really that dry. He throws the question back to the only One for whom this is a genuine open question. That is what faith actually is in a valley like this. Faith is not pretending the bones are not dry. Faith is refusing to conclude that dry bones are the end of the matter when the God who made bones is standing next to you asking.

### II. The Word and the Breath: How God Raises the Dead (Ezekiel 37:4-10)

What God commands next is the heart of the matter, and it is the strangest assignment a preacher ever received. "Prophesy over these bones, and say to them, O dry bones, hear the word of the LORD" (Ezekiel 37:4). Preach. To bones. Command a congregation with no ears to hear the word of the LORD. On its face it is absurd — and it is meant to be, because the absurdity is the theology. God does not raise the dead by spectacle, by technique, by the right emotional atmosphere, or by the persuasive power of the preacher. He raises the dead by his own word spoken over them. "So I prophesied as I was commanded. And as I prophesied, there was a sound, and behold, a rattling, and the bones came together, bone to its bone" (Ezekiel 37:7). Then sinews, then flesh, then skin over the top — "but there was no breath in them" (Ezekiel 37:8). Read that last clause slowly. A whole valley of anatomically complete corpses, perfectly assembled, structurally flawless, and dead. Reformation without life is still death. You can put every bone in the right place and still have a morgue.

Then the second command, and here the Hebrew carries the entire sermon. "Prophesy to the breath; prophesy, son of man, and say to the breath, Thus says the Lord GOD: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live" (Ezekiel 37:9). The word is *ruach* — and in this one chapter it is used for wind, for breath, and for the Spirit of God, a single Hebrew word doing triple duty, and the ambiguity is deliberate. The four winds, the breath of life, and the Spirit of the living God are all pressed into the same word so that no one can miss that what raises the dead is nothing less than God's own Spirit. And when *ruach* enters, the change is instant and total: "and the breath came into them, and they lived and stood on their feet, an exceedingly great army" (Ezekiel 37:10). Not a crowd of survivors. An army — the very thing the valley of the slain had been before it died.

- **A. This is Genesis 2 played a second time.** "Then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature" (Genesis 2:7). Ezekiel is watching creation happen again — the same God, the same divine breath, the same lifeless dust raised to standing, breathing life. The message to the exiles is unmistakable. The God who made humanity from dust in the beginning is not out of options when his people are reduced to dust again. What he did once, over nothing, he can do a second time over the ruins of a nation the surrounding empires had already written off the map.
- **B. The dead are raised by the preached word carried by the Spirit.** That pairing — word and Spirit, prophecy and breath — is not a one-time miracle confined to a vision. It is the permanent architecture of how God gives life. "So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ" (Romans 10:17). The God whom Paul worships is the God "who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist" (Romans 4:17). And when Jesus stood outside a tomb four days sealed, where the sister had already objected that there would be a stench, and "cried out with a loud voice, Lazarus, come out" (John 11:43) — and the dead man came out, still bound in his graveclothes — that was Ezekiel's valley made flesh in a single grave. The word of God spoken over a body the family had already buried and mourned and given up. The method has never once changed. God raises the dead by his word and his breath, and by nothing else.

### III. The Application: Resurrection Hope in a Culture That Has Buried Its Own

God gives the interpretation himself, so we are not left guessing at the meaning. "These bones are the whole house of Israel. Behold, they say, Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost; we are indeed cut off" (Ezekiel 37:11). The valley, it turns out, is not primarily a graveyard. It is a state of mind — the settled, reasonable, evidence-based despair of people for whom the verdict is in and the verdict is death. And here is where a post-Christian West should catch its own reflection in the glass and not look away. We are not a culture that lost God by accident. We are the civilization that conducted the funeral ourselves and signed the certificate. The philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche put the words into the mouth of his madman in 1882, in *The Gay Science* — "God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him." And the crucial thing about that passage, which the people who quote it as a boast always miss, is that Nietzsche was not gloating. His madman is horrified. He is asking who will wipe the blood from our hands, how we can console ourselves now that we have unchained the earth from its sun. He was one of the rare honest atheists who understood that a culture which buries God will, in time, find its own bones drying, its own meaning bleaching on open ground. The sociologist Charles Taylor, in *A Secular Age* in 2007, traced the long, slow arc of exactly that — how the West moved, across five centuries, from a world so soaked in transcendence that unbelief was nearly impossible to a flattened, immanent frame in which belief itself has become, for many, simply one strange option among others. That is our valley. Very many. Very dry.

- **A. The despair is honest, and the church must not lie about it.** I have sat across a table from people whose marriages were not struggling but finished, whose faith was not doubting but gone, who said to me in almost these words, my bones are dried up and my hope is lost. The pastoral temptation in that moment is enormous and it is wrong. The temptation is to argue them out of the diagnosis — to insist the bones are not really that dry, that things are not as bad as they feel, that a little effort will set it right. Do not. The bones are dry. Ezekiel was made to walk the entire valley before God said a word about resurrection. Honesty about the death is not the enemy of resurrection hope. It is the only ground on which resurrection hope means anything at all, because a resurrection is only good news to someone who has admitted there was a death.
- **B. The same word still raises the same kind of dead.** Paul takes Ezekiel's valley and lays it directly over every one of us, with no distance left: "And you were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked... But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved" (Ephesians 2:1-5). Dead, not sick. Made alive, not merely encouraged or coached or motivated. And the same promise runs all the way out to the last day: "the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable" (1 Corinthians 15:52). So the valley of dry bones is not finally a promise about one ancient nation's restoration and nothing more. It is a revelation of the character of God — a God who specializes in the exact cases that everyone else has already closed and filed. The God who breathed life into a slaughtered army and called a four-day corpse out of a sealed tomb will one day breathe over actual graves, over the ones we have visited and left flowers on, and they will stand.

So the question God asked Ezekiel is the question God still asks the church as it stands over its own dead — over a dead culture, over a dead faith, over a dead marriage it has quietly stopped praying for. Can these bones live? The reasonable answer, the answer any honest person gives, is no. The faithful answer is the prophet's answer: O Lord God, you know. And the gospel answer, spoken by the only One who has the right to speak it, is that he will open the graves and raise his people from them and put his Spirit within them, and they shall live and stand in their own land (Ezekiel 37:13-14). The only thing the valley of dry bones needs is a word it cannot possibly say to itself.

These bones can live again.

## Gog and the End of the Threat: The Final Enemy and the Security of God's People (Ezekiel 38-39)
*Why the last enemy is not the one you fear, and what it means that he loses*

**Text:** Ezekiel 38-39 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 38:23 · Psalm 2:1-4 · Romans 8:38-39 · 1 Corinthians 15:26 · Revelation 20:7-9 · Romans 16:20

The most dangerous moment for a restored people is the moment they finally feel safe. You would think, reading Ezekiel in order, that the danger was over. The heart of stone has been removed. The dry bones have stood up as an army. The shepherds who fed themselves have been fired and God himself has taken the flock in hand. And then Ezekiel turns the page, and there is one more enemy — larger than any before, later than all the rest, summoned out of the far uttermost north against a people now living "securely, all of them dwelling without walls, and having no bars or gates" (Ezekiel 38:11). These two strange, war-soaked, difficult chapters exist to answer the specific fear that haunts every redeemed life the morning after the rescue: the nagging suspicion that it is not really final, that some enemy is still out there, somewhere, big enough to undo the whole thing. Ezekiel does not soothe that fear with reassurances. He does something better. He names the ultimate enemy, gathers him to a head, and then has God destroy him so completely that burying the dead takes seven months.

### I. The Enemy Gathered: A Threat Summoned, Not Sovereign (Ezekiel 38:1-16)

Gog of the land of Magog enters the scene as the archetype of every final menace — chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, leading a vast coalition drawn from the edges of the known world: Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer, Beth-togarmah, peoples from the remotest parts (Ezekiel 38:1-6). The names are deliberately distant and shadowy, chosen from the far rim of the map. This is not meant to be a border skirmish with an identifiable local army. This is the last enemy, the accumulated residue of all hostility against the people of God, gathered into one overwhelming figure. And yet notice, before you feel the fear the scene is designed to raise, exactly who does the summoning. "I will turn you about and put hooks into your jaws, and I will bring you out, with all your army" (Ezekiel 38:4). The most fearsome invader in the book is led onto the field by a hook through the jaw, like a fish hauled up on a line by a fisherman who was never in any danger. He comes "in the latter years" against a land restored from war, its people regathered from many nations and dwelling in quiet (Ezekiel 38:8). The picture is exact and intentional: this is a people who thought the fighting was finished, attacked precisely at the point of their assumed security.

- **A. Gog's malice is real; God's purpose overrules it.** Gog is not a puppet with no will of his own. He comes with genuine intent — "to seize spoil and carry off plunder" (Ezekiel 38:12), scheming an evil plan against a peaceful people. The hostility is real, not staged. But over and above that real malice stands a higher and governing intention: "I will bring you against my land, that the nations may know me, when through you, O Gog, I vindicate my holiness before their eyes" (Ezekiel 38:16). Both are fully true at once. The enemy means evil, and God means to be glorified through his defeat, and the second sovereignly governs the first without cancelling it. This is the same logic by which the cross itself would later work — real wickedness, fully intended, wholly overruled.
- **B. This is Psalm 2 set to prophecy.** "Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed... He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision" (Psalm 2:1-4). The raging is loud, the coalition is vast, the horses and the multitude cover the land like a cloud — and heaven is not anxious. Heaven laughs. Gog is the raging of Psalm 2 marched onto Ezekiel's page and given a name, so that the exiles could watch, in advance, exactly how the rage of the nations against God always ends.

### II. The Enemy Destroyed: Total, Public, and Self-Wrought (Ezekiel 38:17-39:20)

The defeat, when it comes, is not a close-run thing, and this is the point Ezekiel labors. There is, strictly, no decisive battle in the human sense at all — no heroic Israelite stand, no clever tactics, no turning of the tide. God himself acts directly. Earthquake, so that the fish and the birds and the mountains shake at his presence. Sword turned inward, "every man's sword will be against his brother" (Ezekiel 38:21), the coalition destroying itself in confusion. Then pestilence and bloodshed, and "torrential rains and hailstones, fire and sulfur" poured out from heaven (Ezekiel 38:22). The enemy that marched in to plunder ends as carrion for the birds. And the aftermath is described with a grim, almost deliberately excessive thoroughness that is its own sermon: Israel burns the abandoned weapons for fuel for seven years and needs no other firewood (Ezekiel 39:9-10), and the burial of the dead takes a full seven months, with search parties appointed to comb the land for stray bones (Ezekiel 39:12-15). The land is not merely spared. It is cleansed down to the last trace, until even the memory of the threat is scrubbed from the ground.

- **A. The whole point is the knowledge of God, repeated like a drumbeat.** The refrain that runs through these two chapters, sounding again and again, is "then they will know that I am the LORD." It falls on Gog, on Israel, on the watching nations. And the climax states the ultimate aim in the plainest terms: "So I will show my greatness and my holiness and make myself known in the eyes of many nations. Then they will know that I am the LORD" (Ezekiel 38:23). The defeat of the final enemy is not finally, at bottom, about Israel's comfort or safety. It is about the name of God being known to the ends of the earth. The security of the people and the glory of God are the same event.
- **B. The last enemy is named in the New Testament, and he loses the very same way.** Paul says it without hedging: "The last enemy to be destroyed is death" (1 Corinthians 15:26). And the book of Revelation takes Ezekiel's own figures — it reaches back and lifts the names straight off the page, "Gog and Magog" — and places them at the very end of history, gathered for the final assault, surrounding the camp of the saints, only for the same verdict to fall: "fire came down from heaven and consumed them" (Revelation 20:7-9). The pattern is line-for-line identical to Ezekiel: the final enemy gathered, the people encircled and outnumbered, and a victory won not by the strength or strategy of the saints but by fire descending from God. The threat that looks final is not final. The God who buried Gog under seven months of graves will one day bury death itself.

### III. The Application: Living Without Bars or Gates in an Age of Fear

Here is what this asks of us, and it is far harder than it first appears. We are not, on the whole, a brave people. The Western church has grown anxious in a manner that would have genuinely puzzled the exiles who first received Ezekiel — anxious about cultural decline, about statistics and attendance, about lost influence and lost privilege, about the next election, the next court ruling, the next cultural shift that might, we fear, finally undo whatever it is we assume we built. And anxiety has a reliable habit of producing exactly the sins it claims to be resisting. We reach for political power because we are afraid. We harden toward the outsider and the stranger because we are afraid. We trade the long patience of the gospel for the short panic of the embattled — because underneath the God-talk, functionally, we do not actually believe the final enemy has already been hooked through the jaw and led onto a field he cannot leave alive.

I know this fear from the inside, not as a diagnosis I deliver to others. I have felt the pull, as a pastor watching the same headlines and the same numbers everyone else watches, to treat the church as a fortress under final siege, to preach as though the survival of the faith itself depended on our vigilance and our victories rather than on the unbreakable name of God. That is functional Gog-anxiety, and it is a quiet, respectable denial of Ezekiel 38. A people who genuinely believed the last enemy loses would live, as the prophecy says of them, "without walls, and having no bars or gates" (Ezekiel 38:11) — not because they naively imagine no enemy exists, but because they know how the story ends, and the ending is already written and signed.

- **A. The early church faced a Gog that looked unbeatable, and outlasted it without a sword.** When the Emperor Diocletian launched the Great Persecution in 303 AD — the most systematic and determined attempt the Roman state ever made to erase the Christian faith, ordering Scriptures burned, church buildings demolished, clergy imprisoned, and believers executed across the empire — it had every appearance of a final enemy come to finish the job. It was empire against a defenseless minority. And within a single generation, by the Edict of Milan in 313 AD, the persecuting empire itself had bent and granted the church toleration. The church did not outlast Diocletian by seizing the levers of Roman power in a panic, or by out-organizing the state, or by winning a war. It outlasted him by dying well, by refusing to hate, by trusting that the One who sits in the heavens laughs at the raging of kings. Every Gog since — every power that rose up certain it would be the one to bury the church — has met precisely the same end, and the church has buried them all.
- **B. The defeat of the last enemy is already secured in the resurrection of Christ.** Paul closes his letter to the Romans with a deliberate echo of both Eden and Ezekiel's coming victory: "The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet" (Romans 16:20). The reason no enemy outlasts the people of God is not that we are strong. It is that the single decisive enemy has already been beaten in the open — death itself was made to walk backwards out of a sealed tomb on Easter morning, defeated not in the last chapter of history but in the middle of it, as a completed fact. And because of that completed fact, Paul can stack every conceivable threat in a single breath and dismiss the whole pile: "neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:38-39). Gog has a hook in his jaw. He always did, from the moment he was summoned.

So the question the chapter leaves with us is not whether enemies will gather. They will; Ezekiel guarantees it and Revelation confirms it, right up to the end. The question is whether we will live like a people whose final enemy has already been defeated and buried, or like a people still frantically bracing for a battle that God has already declared finished. If your faith runs on the panic of the embattled — if it needs the next win to feel secure — then you have not yet believed how this chapter ends. Read it again to the last verse. The fire comes down from heaven. It does not come from us, and it never needed to.

No enemy outlasts God's people.

## The Glory Returns to the Temple: The Presence That Departed Comes Back to Dwell (Ezekiel 40-43)
*What it means that the God who left in judgment returns by the same road*

**Text:** Ezekiel 40-43 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 43:2-4 · Ezekiel 10:18-19 · John 1:14 · John 2:19-21 · Revelation 21:3 · 1 Corinthians 6:19

The worst thing that ever happened to Israel was not the Babylonian army breaking through the wall. It was a quieter thing, years before the siege, and most of the city never even knew it happened. Ezekiel had been shown it in a vision: the glory of God rose from above the cherubim in the temple, paused at the threshold as if reluctant, moved to the east gate, and then lifted from the city entirely and stood on the mountain to the east (Ezekiel 10-11). That was the real catastrophe. The judgment was not fundamentally the sword and the fire and the deportation. The judgment was that God left. Everything else was only the consequence of an empty room. So when, in the twenty-fifth year of the exile (Ezekiel 40:1), the prophet is given a long, patient, almost exhausting vision of a measured temple — gate by gate, wall by wall, cubit by careful cubit — the reader who has been paying attention through the whole book is waiting for one thing and one thing only. Not the architecture. The return of the One who left.

### I. The Measured Temple: Order Restored With Painstaking Care (Ezekiel 40-42)

For three long chapters, a figure "whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze" leads Ezekiel through a temple, a measuring reed in his hand, recording every gate, threshold, chamber, pillar, and court with relentless precision (Ezekiel 40:3). To a modern reader it can feel interminable, a stretch of Scripture we are tempted to skim. But put yourself inside the head of an exile who had personally watched, or heard the eyewitness reports of, the temple of Solomon reduced to ash and rubble. To that person, every single measurement was a promise with weight. A God who bothers to measure a building intends to build it. The painstaking, tedious detail is not divine bureaucracy; it is a form of tenderness — the care of a God who is recording, down to the last cubit, the house he fully means to fill again. Nothing here is approximate. Nothing is left to chance, because nothing about this restoration is going to be accidental or fragile.

- **A. The order itself preaches.** Recall the problem back in chapters 8 through 11, where Ezekiel had been shown the abominations hidden inside the temple precincts — elders worshiping creatures in the dark, women weeping for Tammuz, men bowing to the sun with their backs to the sanctuary. Defilement had corrupted the very house of God from the inside. Now, in the vision, everything is squared, walled, measured, carefully set apart, "to make a separation between the holy and the common" (Ezekiel 42:20). The vision answers the earlier defilement one measurement at a time. What sin had disordered and profaned, God reorders and re-consecrates. Holiness is being rebuilt with the same care with which it had been violated.
- **B. The structure waits for an occupant.** And yet, for all its flawless precision, the temple of chapters 40 through 42 is empty. This matters enormously and is easy to miss in the flood of measurements. A perfect house with no resident is not yet good news; it is a monument, at best a memorial. The whole long, patient vision leans forward, unfinished and unresolved, toward a single event it has deliberately withheld. The One for whom the entire house was measured has not yet arrived. The building is holding its breath.

### II. The Glory Returns By the Eastern Way (Ezekiel 43:1-5)

Then comes the moment the entire book has been driving toward since the glory departed in chapter 10. "Then he led me to the gate, the gate facing east. And behold, the glory of the God of Israel was coming from the east. And the sound of his coming was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with his glory" (Ezekiel 43:1-2). Ezekiel — the same prophet who had been forced, years before, to stand and watch the glory leave — now sees it return, and he cannot contain the recognition. He names the connection himself, urgently: "And the vision I saw was just like the vision that I had seen when he came to destroy the city, and just like the vision that I had seen by the Chebar canal" (Ezekiel 43:3). Same glory. Same God. Not a lesser presence, not a symbol, not a memory — the identical glory he had seen depart and had first seen by the river in his call vision. And then the sentence the whole book was written to reach: "As the glory of the LORD entered the temple by the gate facing east... behold, the glory of the LORD filled the temple" (Ezekiel 43:4-5).

- **A. The road back is the road out, exactly reversed.** Go back and read it against the departure. In Ezekiel 10:18-19, "the glory of the LORD went out from the threshold of the house and stood over the cherubim," and the cherubim rose and "stood at the entrance of the east gate of the house of the LORD." By the east gate the glory left. By the east gate the glory returns. God does not slip back in quietly through some side door, hoping the exile will be forgotten. He returns by the very same road he departed, in full view, undoing the departure step for step, so that the return is unmistakably the reversal of the judgment and not merely a fresh arrival. The presence that left in wrath comes back to dwell.
- **B. And this time God binds himself to stay.** From within the filled temple, a voice sets out the terms: "Son of man, this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever" (Ezekiel 43:7). Forever. The glory that had proved, in chapter 10, that it could leave — that God is not trapped in any building and will abandon a house that has become an idol — now freely pledges permanence. The entire arc of the book resolves in this one word. Glory departing, judgment falling, bones rising, the final enemy defeated, and now the presence returning to live among his people and swearing never to leave them again.

### III. The Application: Where the Returned Glory Now Dwells

This is where the vision reaches us, and where it costs more than sentiment. A post-Christian culture is, at its root, a culture from which the glory has lifted. The West is a society that still has the architecture of Christendom all around it — the cathedrals on the skyline, the holy days on the calendar, the borrowed moral vocabulary of dignity and compassion and human rights that it can no longer quite explain — but increasingly without the resident presence that once filled and animated all of it. The philosopher Charles Taylor, in *A Secular Age* in 2007, described the modern West as "disenchanted," the transcendent quietly withdrawn behind a flattened immanent frame, until for many people the felt absence of God has simply become the ordinary texture of reality. That is precisely the temple of Ezekiel 40 through 42 without chapter 43: a beautifully measured, historically impressive structure, the cultural shell of a faith, standing empty. And here is the sharp temptation for the church in an age like ours: to fight for the shell. To pour our energy into recovering the architecture — the prayer restored to the schoolroom, the symbols kept in the public square, the general Christian tone of the culture — as though recovering the building were the same thing as recovering the glory. It is not. An empty temple, however ornate, however historic, is still an empty temple.

I have done this myself, more than I would like to admit. I have grieved the loss of cultural Christian privilege and standing as though it were the loss of God's actual presence, when the two are not remotely the same thing. The glory does not return because we successfully defend or restore its building. The glory returns because God chooses to come — and the whole staggering news of the gospel is bound up in where, and how, he chose to come.

- **A. The glory returned, and it had a face.** "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth" (John 1:14). The verb John reaches for is *eskenosen* — he tabernacled, he pitched his tent, he made his dwelling. It is temple language, presence language, the vocabulary of the glory that filled the sanctuary. The glory that had filled Ezekiel's visionary temple took on flesh and blood and walked into the world, and it is no small thing that the shepherds and the magi and later the Palm Sunday crowds all approached Jerusalem, fittingly, from the east. And when his enemies demanded a sign of his authority, Jesus answered, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." John, in case anyone should miss it, tells us plainly: "he was speaking about the temple of his body" (John 2:19-21). The measured house of Ezekiel was always, from the first cubit, pointing past stone to a Person.
- **B. And now the glory dwells in the most unlikely temple of all — us.** Paul presses the astonishing conclusion onto an ordinary, struggling, deeply flawed church in Corinth: "Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?" (1 Corinthians 6:19). The glory that departed from Jerusalem, that returned in the flesh of Christ, now fills, by the Spirit, the gathered and indwelt people of God. The early church understood, against every instinct to rebuild a holy building, that everything depended on whether this presence was truly God. That is what the Council of Nicaea was defending in 325 AD when it confessed the Son to be "true God from true God" — not merely a great teacher, not a lesser creature sent as a symbol, but the very glory itself, returned in person. Because if the One who dwelt among us were anything less than God, then the glory had not actually come back at all. It had. It dwells. And the whole vision finds its last resolution where all of Scripture ends: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people" (Revelation 21:3).

So do not spend your grief, or your best energy, on the empty shell. The question that matters is not whether the culture will rebuild the outward architecture of Christendom; it may not, and its bare cathedrals may stand empty for another century. The question is whether the glory dwells in you — and whether a watching, disenchanted world, walking past the churches it no longer enters, might catch sight of the presence it has stopped believing in, not in a building at all, but in a people God came back to fill. The glory that left does not, in the end, depend on us to summon it home. It depends entirely on the God who came back by the eastern road, in the flesh, and pledged forever that he would never leave again.

The glory that left returns.

## The River and the Name of the City: The Healing Presence of God and 'The LORD Is There' (Ezekiel 47-48)
*How the whole vision resolves in a river that heals and a name that holds*

**Text:** Ezekiel 47-48 · **Supporting:** Ezekiel 48:35 · Genesis 2:10 · John 7:37-38 · Revelation 22:1-2 · Psalm 46:4 · Revelation 21:3

A book that opened with a man in exile, convinced everything was finished, ends with a river and a name. That is not a soft, sentimental landing tacked on to relieve the reader after so many chapters of judgment. It is the whole argument of the book resolving into its final chord. Ezekiel has walked us the full length of the descent and the climb — the glory departing, the city burning, the bones drying in the valley, the final enemy gathering in the north — and now, in the closing vision, water begins to trickle out from beneath the threshold of the restored temple, and it refuses to stay a trickle. It deepens as it goes, until no one can cross it, and everything it touches comes alive. And then the very last word of the entire prophecy — fifty chapters of desolation and restoration compressed into a single name — is the new name given to the city: *Yahweh Shammah*. The LORD is there. That name is where the whole book was going from its first verse by the Chebar canal.

### I. The River From the Threshold: Life Where God Dwells (Ezekiel 47:1-12)

The water has a source, and the source is the entire point of the vision. "Then he brought me back to the door of the temple, and behold, water was issuing from below the threshold of the temple toward the east" (Ezekiel 47:1). It does not rise from a spring in the hills or fall from a cloud. It flows out from directly beneath the house where, just a few chapters earlier, the glory of God had returned to dwell. The river is not produced by the land at all; it flows out from the presence of God himself, and it grows in a way that no natural river ever grows — without a single tributary feeding it. The guide leads Ezekiel out and measures as they go. A thousand cubits, and the water is ankle-deep. Another thousand, and it is knee-deep. Another thousand, and it reaches the waist. Another, and "it was a river that I could not pass through, for the water had risen. It was deep enough to swim in, a river that could not be passed through" (Ezekiel 47:5). Grace that deepens the farther it travels from its source, drawing on nothing but where it began.

- **A. Where the river goes, death itself turns to life.** It runs down through the Arabah and empties into the sea — and the sea in view is the Dead Sea, the saltiest, most lifeless body of water in the region, so mineral-choked that nothing lives in it. And when the river reaches even that, "the water will become fresh. So everything will live where the river goes" (Ezekiel 47:8-9). Fishermen will stand along its banks from En-gedi to En-eglaim, spreading their nets, and the fish will be of very many kinds (Ezekiel 47:10). The single most dead place on the map becomes the most teeming with life. The river does not avoid the Dead Sea. The river specializes in it.
- **B. The trees on its banks never fail.** "And on the banks, on both sides of the river, there will grow all kinds of trees for food. Their leaves will not wither, nor their fruit fail, but they will bear fresh fruit every month, because the water for them flows from the sanctuary. Their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing" (Ezekiel 47:12). Note carefully the reason the text itself supplies for this unfailing fruitfulness: *because the water for them flows from the sanctuary.* The healing power is not in the trees, and it is not in the soil. It is in the source. Cut off from the sanctuary, the banks would be desert; connected to it, they cannot stop bearing.

### II. The River Runs the Whole Length of Scripture (Genesis to Revelation)

Ezekiel's river is not a stand-alone marvel dropped into one prophet's vision. It is a single thread the whole Bible has been pulling from the first garden to the last city. "A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and there it divided" (Genesis 2:10) — life flowing out from the place of God's presence, before human rebellion barred the way back and posted the cherubim at the gate. The Psalms sang of this same river in the dark of national crisis: "There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High" (Psalm 46:4). And the book of Revelation, closing the entire canon, takes Ezekiel's vision and opens it into its final and permanent form: "Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of the street of the city; also, on either side of the river, the tree of life... and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations" (Revelation 22:1-2). It is the same river, the same trees on both banks, the same leaves for healing — Ezekiel 47 stretched out to eternity and traced back to its true throne. What the prophet saw in a vision, John saw as the final reality.

- **A. The river is finally a Person.** Jesus stood up on the last and greatest day of the Feast of Booths, in the temple courts, and made the claim that gathers every strand of this to himself: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water" (John 7:37-38). And John, so we do not mistake the image for poetry, adds the interpretation directly: "Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive" (John 7:39). The river that flows from the threshold of Ezekiel's temple flows, in the end, from Christ — the true temple, the true source — and then, astonishingly, through his Spirit from the hearts of those who come to him and drink. The healing water has a name, and the name is Jesus.
- **B. The Dead Sea is the gospel's natural home.** A river that turns the saltiest, deadest, most hopeless water fresh and fills it with life is the precise picture of what God does with the people and the places the world has already written off as beyond reviving. Wherever the river goes, everything lives. The question the chapter presses on us is not whether the water is able to heal — it plainly is — but whether we will let it reach the parts of us we long ago decided were our own private Dead Sea, the corners of a marriage or a memory or a besetting sin that we have quietly given up on. And whether the church will actually carry this river out to the places, and the people, everyone else has declared beyond saving.

### III. The Application: 'The LORD Is There' in a Disenchanted World

The book does not end with the river. It ends with a name, and the name is the resolution of everything that came before it. After all the careful tribal allotments and the twelve gates of the city named for the twelve tribes in chapter 48, the final verse of the whole prophecy lands its last word: "And the name of the city from that time on shall be, The LORD Is There" (Ezekiel 48:35) — *Yahweh Shammah*. Sit with the weight of that against the arc of the book. The whole catastrophe had been, at its root, an absence: the glory that left, the city God had abandoned to the sword because it had first abandoned him. And the whole hope of the book is, at its root, a presence. Not the LORD will eventually fix it. Not the LORD approves of what we have made. Simply: the LORD is there. Everything the exiles had lost is restored in those three syllables, because everything they had truly lost, underneath the temple and the land and the throne, was him.

This is precisely the word a post-Christian West has lost the very capacity to want. The philosopher Charles Taylor, in *A Secular Age* in 2007, described the modern self as "buffered" — sealed off from transcendence, no longer porous to the presence and the power of God the way earlier ages were, living inside a world where his absence has come to feel like the normal, default, self-evident state of things. We have built an entire civilization on the exact opposite of *Yahweh Shammah*: the settled assumption that the LORD is not here, and a quiet, half-conscious preference for keeping it that way, because his real absence conveniently leaves us in charge of our own lives. And the church, drinking from the same disenchanted water without noticing, often settles for a Christianity of activity, technique, and management that could run along perfectly well whether God ever showed up or not.

- **A. I have built ministry that did not actually need God to be there.** I say this as confession, not observation. I have planned services, written sermons, and run programs that would have proceeded exactly the same, with the same efficiency and the same applause, if the glory had never once returned to the temple — a competent religion of human effort with God installed as the absent guest of honor. That is the empty city before it is given its new name. The single thing that finally distinguishes the people of God from a well-run and well-meaning nonprofit is not the quality of our strategy or the warmth of our community. It is whether the LORD is there. Strip that away, and however impressive the operation, we are back in an empty temple with the glory long departed.
- **B. The early church staked everything on the presence, not the program.** When Athanasius fought through the whole of the fourth century — often alone, exiled five times, standing against the combined weight of emperors and councils in the years around and after the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD — to insist that the Son was truly God and not an exalted creature, he was, at bottom, contending for *Yahweh Shammah* in the flesh. Because if Christ were merely a noble creature, however high, then God had not actually come to dwell among us at all, and the river had no true source, and the healing was a rumor. The church grasped, with its life, that everything hung on whether God was really and personally present in Christ. He was. And so the canon closes not with a strategy or even a victory but with a presence made permanent and universal: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God" (Revelation 21:3).

So the thing Ezekiel finally leaves us holding, at the end of all his visions of wheels and bones and glory and rivers, is the simplest and the hardest question there is. Not whether your life is well-ordered. Not whether the outward architecture of your faith is in good repair. But whether the LORD is there — in your home, in your prayers, in the church you are giving your life to build, in the dead places you long ago stopped carrying to the river. The whole book was a movement from a glory that could leave to a presence that will not. If the river truly runs from the throne, then nothing it reaches stays dead. And the very last word spoken over the city of God is not a plan, not a program, not a triumph. It is a presence.

The LORD is there.
